# INTRODUCTION

This chapter presents the research foundation of the study. It explains why one model for humanitarian classification and named entity recognition (NER) of Taglish disaster posts is worth developing, and why the choice of multi-task optimizer matters for such a model. It then states the research questions, hypotheses, frameworks, and boundaries that guide the rest of the study.

## Introduction to the Study

Natural language processing (NLP), the field of computer science that develops methods for computers to process human language, can help responders use information from social media during disasters [@lewis2025tapping]. This help matters in the Philippines, which has the highest disaster risk among 193 countries [@bundnis2025worldriskreport]. During tropical cyclones, Filipinos post their needs and calls for help on social media, often in Taglish, and these posts arrive in larger numbers than responders can review one by one [@inoferio2025socialmedia; @montalan2025batayan; @somido2023actionable]. Two NLP tasks could sort them. Humanitarian classification identifies the type of report in each post [@alam2021humaid], and NER finds details such as locations and requested supplies [@ali2026humaidner]. No Taglish dataset reviewed here, however, labels the same posts for both tasks. One model that performs both tasks, called a multi-task model, is expected to save storage and processing time compared with two separate models [@wang2021transformer; @ali2026humaidner], but it can perform worse on a task than a model trained on that task alone, a problem known as negative transfer [@mueller2022taskconflict]. Training methods called multi-task optimizers are meant to reduce this problem, but studies disagree on whether they work better than treating both tasks equally [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform], and none of the studies reviewed here tested them on Taglish posts. This study therefore develops one multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, rather than combining two existing models. The model only sorts each post into a humanitarian category and marks key details in it, such as locations and requested supplies, without correcting or rewriting the post. The study also builds a Taglish typhoon dataset annotated for both tasks, benchmarks 13 multi-task optimizers on negative transfer and on training cost, which is the time and memory that training needs, and compares the final model with two single-task models, one for each task. It contributes the dataset, the model, and evidence on whether multi-task optimizers help when one task labels whole posts and the other labels individual words.

## Background of the Study

Part of this risk comes from the high exposure of the country to extreme weather [@bundnis2025worldriskreport]. Tropical cyclones are one form of extreme weather, and about eight or nine cross the country each year, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone]. During these cyclones, Filipinos post their needs, report damage, and call for help on social media [@inoferio2025socialmedia; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Many of these posts are written in Taglish, because Filipinos often switch between Tagalog and English on social media [@montalan2025batayan; @ermino2022urgency]. These posts arrive in such large numbers that responders cannot review them one by one [@somido2023actionable; @wang2021transformer]. Responders therefore need automated tools that can sort Taglish posts.

Such a tool must tell responders what kind of report each post is and what details it gives, such as where help is needed and what supplies are asked for [@ali2026humaidner; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Two tasks in NLP provide this information. Humanitarian classification assigns each post one category, such as requests for help or reports of damaged roads and buildings, from a set chosen for its usefulness to humanitarian organizations [@alam2021humaid]. NER finds details within the post, such as locations and requested supplies [@yute2021satellite; @ali2026humaidner]. The two tasks complement each other, because a category alone does not say where help is needed or what is asked for [@ali2026humaidner].

Despite this, most of the Philippine studies reviewed here trained a model for only one task. Ermino et al. [-@ermino2022urgency] classified posts by urgency, Somido and Reyes [-@somido2023actionable] classified them by whether they were informative, and Yute et al. [-@yute2021satellite] found locations in them. A recent system for Urdaneta City performs both tasks by sending the comments to a large language model (LLM) [@caoile2025urdaneta]. Training one model to perform both tasks on Taglish posts requires a dataset in which the same posts are labeled for both tasks. Such a dataset exists for English posts [@ali2026humaidner], but none of the datasets reviewed in Chapter 2 does the same for Taglish. This gap reflects a wider shortage, since Tagalog and Taglish have far fewer labeled datasets than English [@cruz2022tagalog; @herrera2022tweettaglish; @montalan2025batayan].

With a Taglish dataset labeled for both tasks, a tool that provides both outputs could be built on a pretrained encoder, a language model that has already learned from large amounts of text. Pretrained encoders are much smaller than LLMs, yet once trained on labeled examples, they often classify text as well as or better than LLMs that are only given instructions [@bucher2024finetuned], including posts about disasters [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot]. The tool could use two separate models, one for each task, each with its own pretrained encoder. A multi-task model instead shares one pretrained encoder between both tasks, so it is expected to need less storage space and processing time than two separate models [@lin2023libmtl; @wang2021transformer].

However, a multi-task model can perform worse on a task than a single-task model, which is a model trained on that task alone. In other words, its predictive performance, which is how accurately it predicts the labels of that task, can be lower. This problem is called negative transfer [@mueller2022taskconflict; @elich2024paradigms]. If the loss is large, the savings in storage and processing time come at the cost of less accurate outputs, such as requests for help sorted into the wrong category. There are reasons to expect negative transfer when classification and NER share one model. During training, each task sends the model a signal, called a task gradient, that shows how the model should change. On English text, @zhu2025prefinetuning found that the two tasks sent the model conflicting signals and that each task performed slightly worse than when trained alone. Ali et al. [-@ali2026humaidner] argued that the task gradient of NER may overpower that of classification, because NER makes a decision for every word in a post while classification makes only one decision for the whole post.

Both point to the way the two tasks influence the model during training. Multi-task optimizers are training methods that control this influence, and most of them aim to reduce negative transfer. The simplest optimizers keep the task weights, the numbers that set how strongly each task influences the model, fixed throughout training. Equal weighting gives both tasks the same weight, and tuned static weighting uses weights chosen by testing several options before training. The other optimizers, which some studies call specialized optimizers [@hu2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform], adjust the task weights during training, change the task gradients, or do both [@elich2024paradigms]. Studies disagree on whether these other optimizers perform better than fixed task weights. Several found that fixed task weights performed as well or better [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization]. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform], however, found that the other optimizers performed about the same as equal weighting on simple problems with similar tasks, while most of them outperformed it on more complex problems.

The optimizers also differ in training cost. Many of the other optimizers compute each task gradient separately at every training step, which takes more time and memory [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. This cost is paid again each time the model is retrained, which may be needed after new disasters, since models trained on posts from past disasters often perform worse on new ones [@seeberger2025generalizing]. Computing resources are also costly for many researchers, especially those in emerging economies [@schwartz2020green; @treviso2023efficient]. None of the studies reviewed here compared these optimizers on negative transfer or training cost for classification and NER of Taglish posts, so the best choice for these tasks cannot be known in advance and has to be tested.

## Statement of the Problem

This study aims to design, implement, and empirically evaluate a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to choose its multi-task optimizer based on negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, it answers four research questions.

1. What is the predictive performance of single-task models for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts? (Baseline Analysis)

2. How can a multi-task model be designed to perform both humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts? (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. Which of the 13 multi-task optimizers should the final model use, based on negative transfer and training cost? (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. How does the final multi-task model compare with the single-task models in predictive performance, training time, peak memory, storage, and processing time? (Comparative Validation)

## Objectives

The general objective is to develop a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. To support this, the study first builds a Taglish dataset labeled for both tasks. Specifically, the study pursues four objectives.

1. To measure the predictive performance of single-task models for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts. (Baseline Analysis)

2. To design and implement a multi-task model that performs both humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. To select the multi-task optimizer for the final model by comparing the negative transfer of the 13 candidate models on the validation posts and their training cost. (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. To compare the final multi-task model with the single-task models in predictive performance, training time, peak memory, storage, and processing time. (Comparative Validation)

## Hypotheses

The study tests the following null and alternative hypotheses for each of the two tasks on the test posts.

**Null hypothesis ($H_0$).** The mean predictive performance across training runs is the same for the final multi-task model and the single-task model for that task.

**Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$).** The mean predictive performance across training runs differs between the final multi-task model and the single-task model for that task.

## Theoretical Framework

This study is grounded in the view of multi-task learning as inductive transfer, a term that Caruana [-@caruana1997multitask] used for the idea that what a model learns for one task can help it learn a related task. Humanitarian classification and NER of disaster posts are related in this way, because the details that NER finds are often the same evidence that shows the category of a post. For example, a post in which NER finds a request such as "need food" is likely to belong to the category for requests or urgent needs, and a post that mentions "1,000 evacuees" is likely to belong to the category for displaced people and evacuations [@alam2021humaid; @ali2026humaidner]. When this sharing helps, the multi-task model performs better on a task than a single-task model. This gain is called positive transfer. When one task interferes with the other, the multi-task model performs worse. This loss is negative transfer. Multi-task models that process text have shown both [@mueller2022taskconflict]. In other cases, neither effect was strong. @zou2025typhoon trained one model to find place names in Chinese text and to classify damage in Chinese posts about typhoons, a pairing similar to the one in this study. In their basic multi-task model, the predictive performance of each task changed by less than one percentage point compared with two separate models. The final multi-task model may therefore perform better than, worse than, or about the same as a single-task model on each task. The alternative hypothesis covers the first two outcomes, and the null hypothesis covers the third. In this way, the theory links one independent variable of this study, the type of model, to its dependent variable, predictive performance.

Negative transfer is often traced to two problems with the task gradients [@mueller2022taskconflict]. In gradient conflict, the two task gradients point in directions that work against each other, so a change that helps one task harms the other [@yu2020pcgrad]. In gradient dominance, one task gradient is much larger than the other, so that task controls most of how the model changes [@chen2018gradnorm]. The findings described in the Background of the Study suggest that both may occur between classification and NER. Apart from equal weighting and tuned static weighting, the multi-task optimizers act on these causes by adjusting the task weights during training, by changing the task gradients, or by doing both [@elich2024paradigms]. One theoretical study also showed that, in simple models that are too small for their tasks, fixed task weights cannot reach some results that balance the two tasks [@hu2023scalarization]. The choice of optimizer may therefore change how much negative transfer remains, which links the other independent variable, the multi-task optimizer, to negative transfer. This expectation is the reason the study compares 13 candidate models before selecting the final one. A competing view holds that the choice matters little, because fixed task weights have often performed as well as or better than the other optimizers [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization]. This view is why equal weighting serves as the reference in the selection and why the final model uses it when no other optimizer qualifies.

## Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework uses the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model to show how the study will be carried out. Following the theoretical framework, the study has two independent variables. The multi-task optimizer differs among the 13 candidate models, and its dependent variables are negative transfer and training cost. The type of model, which is either the final multi-task model or a single-task model, differs in the final comparison, and its main dependent variable is predictive performance, which the hypotheses test.

![Research workflow of the study](figures/fig-1-1-research-workflow-ipo.pdf){#fig-research-ipo}

@fig-research-ipo shows the research workflow. The inputs are the Taglish posts, the label definitions of HumAID and HUMAID-NER, the pretrained encoder, the 13 multi-task optimizers, and the laptop used for all training. The study first builds the dataset. Public Taglish posts are collected and cleaned, two annotators label each post, their agreement is measured, and the posts are split into training, validation, and test posts. Next, one single-task model is trained for each task to set the baseline predictive performance (RQ1). The multi-task model is then designed so that both tasks share the pretrained encoder, as @fig-artifact-ipo shows (RQ2). Thirteen candidate versions of this model are trained, one for each optimizer. They share the same encoder, dataset, and laptop, and the learning rate of each is chosen in the same way, so the optimizer is the only planned difference between them. Their negative transfer on the validation posts and their training cost decide which optimizer the final model uses, by the rule described in Chapter 3 (RQ3). Finally, the final model is compared with the single-task models (RQ4). Its predictive performance and processing time are measured on the test posts, and its training time, peak memory, and storage are also compared. The hypotheses are tested on predictive performance, the dependent variable. The output is the final outcome of the study, a multi-task model for both tasks that is trained with the selected optimizer.

![How the multi-task model processes an example post](figures/fig-1-2-artifact-ipo.pdf){#fig-artifact-ipo}

@fig-artifact-ipo shows how the multi-task model handles an example post. The post is first split into smaller units called tokens. The pretrained encoder, which both tasks share, then reads the tokens and converts them into numbers. Two task heads, each a part of the model that makes the predictions for one task, use these numbers. One task head assigns the post a humanitarian category, and the other finds the words that name details such as locations and resources. The encoder reads the post only once to produce both outputs. The post was written for this illustration and is not from the dataset. The figure does not show the optimizer because it acts only during training, where it determines how the two task gradients are combined to update the pretrained encoder.

## Scope and Delimitations

### Scope of the Study

The study covers Taglish posts about tropical cyclones that crossed the Philippines between 2020 and 2026. The word "typhoon" in the title follows its common use in the Philippines, where it refers to any tropical cyclone. Likewise, "Tweets" in the title refers to posts on X, formerly Twitter, which is the main source of the dataset, although public Facebook posts may be added as the Delimitations describe. Every post in the dataset is labeled with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID, and the words in it are labeled with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER. The dataset is planned to give at least 2,801 training posts, or about 3,900 labeled posts in total (Chapter 3).

The study trains 15 model configurations on this dataset. Two single-task models, one for each task, provide the baseline. The multi-task model shares the pretrained encoder between two task heads, one for each task. Thirteen candidate versions of this model are trained, one for each multi-task optimizer, and the candidate trained with the selected optimizer becomes the final model of the study. The 13 optimizers are equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary], tuned static weighting [@xin2022mtohelp], random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw], uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty], gradient normalization (GradNorm) [@chen2018gradnorm], the multiple-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) [@sener2018mgda], projecting conflicting gradients (PCGrad) [@yu2020pcgrad], gradient sign dropout (GradDrop) [@chen2020graddrop], impartial multi-task learning (IMTL) [@liu2021imtl], conflict-averse gradient descent (CAGrad) [@liu2021cagrad], Nash multi-task learning (Nash-MTL) [@navon2022bargaining], fast adaptive multitask optimization (FAMO) [@liu2023famo], and PCGrad with uncertainty weighting [@yu2020pcgrad; @kendall2018uncertainty]. All models use one pretrained encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was trained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

The study measures the inter-annotator agreement of the labels. For every model, it measures predictive performance, training time, and peak memory. For the final model and the single-task models, it also measures storage and processing time. For each candidate model, it also computes negative transfer. Each candidate model is trained three times with different random seeds, and the final model and the two single-task models are trained five times, all on one laptop whose NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU has 8 GB of memory. Before these runs, each model is trained a few more times to choose its learning rate, and tuned static weighting is also trained further times to choose its task weights. These tuning runs are not counted in training cost, but their time is reported separately. Chapter 3 describes the data source, the labeling process, the hardware, the training configuration, the selection rule, and which training run becomes the final model.

The study also builds a prototype web application that runs the final model, to show how staff of a local disaster risk reduction and management office could use it to sort posts. The prototype is tested only to confirm that each of its functions works.

### Delimitations of the Study

**Social media platform.** The dataset uses posts from X, formerly Twitter, because earlier Philippine and international disaster datasets also use posts from Twitter [@ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @alam2021humaid], so the results can be compared with theirs. Public Facebook posts are added only if X does not provide enough Taglish posts, as described in Chapter 3, and the number of posts from each platform is reported. Other platforms are excluded.

**Language.** The dataset covers Taglish only. Other Philippine languages, such as Cebuano and Waray, are excluded because results from a mix of languages would not show whether the model and its optimizer work the same way in each one. Labeling posts in more languages also exceeds the resources of this study.

**Hazard.** The dataset includes tropical cyclones only, which cross the Philippines about eight or nine times a year [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone]. Zou et al. [-@zou2025typhoon] similarly built their dataset from typhoons only, describing China as one of the most typhoon-prone countries in the world. Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other hazards are excluded.

**Time period.** The dataset covers events from 2020 to 2026, the most recent years at the time of the study. Earlier events, such as Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) in 2013, are excluded.

**Modality.** The study includes text only. Images, video, and audio are excluded because both tasks in this study are defined on text.

**Tasks.** The study covers only humanitarian classification and NER. Other tasks, such as sentiment, emotion, or urgency detection, are excluded because adding tasks would change how the tasks interfere with one another, and differences in negative transfer would then be harder to attribute to the optimizers. Excluding them does not imply that they are less useful to responders.

**Multi-task optimizers.** The study compares 13 optimizers. Most were evaluated in earlier studies that compared other optimizers with equal weighting [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @royer2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform], so the results can be compared with theirs. Ali et al. [-@ali2026humaidner] described uncertainty weighting, PCGrad, and GradNorm as complementary for disaster posts and suggested combining PCGrad with uncertainty weighting. Other optimizers are excluded to keep the number of training runs feasible on a single laptop.

**Pretrained encoder.** The study uses one pretrained encoder for all models. Testing other pretrained encoders is excluded because a different encoder would introduce another variable besides the optimizer.

**Training settings.** All models use the same training settings, described in Chapter 3, except the learning rate, which is tuned for each model on the validation posts. The learning rate is the only setting that the benchmarks of Xin et al. [-@xin2022mtohelp], Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary], and Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] all tuned for every optimizer. The settings that belong to each optimizer follow the values of their authors or of LibMTL, a published software library for multi-task learning [@lin2023libmtl], and are not tuned, as in the benchmark of Lin et al. [-@lin2022rlw]. The task weights of tuned static weighting are the exception, because choosing them is what defines that optimizer.

**Training hardware.** All training and measurement are performed on a single laptop. Cloud servers and other machines are excluded so that the training time and peak memory of every optimizer are measured under the same conditions. Because the graphics processor of this laptop has 8 GB of memory, the embedding layer of the encoder, which turns each token into numbers, is not trained in any model, so that all 13 optimizers fit in this memory (Chapter 3).

**Test data.** The study evaluates all models only on posts from its own Taglish dataset. Other disaster datasets, such as the English HUMAID-NER dataset [@ali2026humaidner], are not used for evaluation because differences in language and labeling would change the scores for reasons unrelated to the models being compared.

**Large language models.** The study does not compare the final model with LLMs. The research questions compare multi-task and single-task models built on the same pretrained encoder. An LLM differs from these models in size, training, and cost, so a comparison with it would answer a different question. Earlier studies have already compared smaller trained models with LLMs on classification [@bucher2024finetuned; @mcdaniel2024zeroshot].

**Deployment.** The study develops the final model and evaluates it on test posts only. Use by emergency responders during actual disasters is excluded because the research questions concern how the model is designed, trained, and evaluated, not how responders use it.

**Prototype.** The prototype is not evaluated for usability or tested with the staff of disaster risk reduction and management offices, because the research questions concern the model, not the application that presents it.

## Significance of the Study

**Primary beneficiaries.** Local government units (LGUs) and their disaster risk reduction and management offices gain a model that identifies both the type of report and its details in Taglish posts and that could run on a laptop like the one used in this study, without sending the posts to a paid LLM service. The study reports how the final model compares with the single-task models in predictive performance on each task and in storage and processing time, which shows what an office would gain or give up by running one model instead of two. The prototype shows how office staff could use the model to sort posts. Local universities and research groups also benefit, since the training time and peak memory show what they would need to build and update the model for these offices.

**Secondary beneficiaries.** Researchers in NLP and crisis informatics, the study of how information from social media can support disaster response, and developers of multi-task models gain a Taglish dataset labeled for both tasks and a benchmark of 13 multi-task optimizers on Taglish disaster posts. The benchmark shows whether any optimizer differs from equal weighting in negative transfer and how much training time and memory each needs. This adds evidence to the debate on whether the other optimizers outperform equal weighting, since the comparisons of several optimizers reviewed here did not use Taglish text or pair a task that labels a whole post with one that labels each word. The study also provides its code and labeling guidelines, which later studies can use to build similar datasets or to add tasks such as emotion detection. The final model and the labeled dataset are shared only in forms that data privacy rules and the terms of the platforms allow. The dataset, for example, is shared as a list of post IDs instead of the posts themselves.

**Tertiary beneficiaries.** Communities affected by tropical cyclones could benefit indirectly. If responders adopt the final model, they may identify urgent requests for rescue and relief more quickly among the large number of incoming posts.

## Definitions of Terms

The following terms are defined as they are used in this study.

**Candidate model.** One of the 13 versions of the multi-task model, each trained with a different multi-task optimizer. The final model is selected from them.

**Equal weighting.** The multi-task optimizer that gives both tasks the same task weight, which stays fixed throughout training. It is the reference against which the other optimizers are compared.

**F1-score.** A score between 0 and 1 that combines precision and recall, computed on the validation or test posts. Humanitarian classification uses macro-F1, which gives every category equal weight, and NER uses span-level micro-F1, which counts an entity as correct only when its boundaries and its type both match the label. Chapter 3 gives the formulas.

**Final model.** The candidate model trained with the multi-task optimizer selected under the third research question. It is the main outcome of the study. Chapter 3 describes which of its training runs is used.

**Gradient conflict.** The case in which the two task gradients point in directions that work against each other, so a change that helps one task harms the other.

**Gradient dominance.** The case in which one task gradient is much larger than the other, so the model changes mostly in the direction that the task with the larger gradient needs.

**Humanitarian classification.** The task that assigns each post one category naming the kind of information it reports, such as a request for supplies or damaged infrastructure.

**Inter-annotator agreement.** The degree to which different annotators assign the same label to the same post or word, which shows how consistently the dataset is labeled. Chapter 3 describes how it is measured.

**Label.** The category or entity type that annotators assign to a post, or to a word in a post, which the models learn from and are tested against.

**Multi-task model.** A model with one pretrained encoder shared by both tasks and a task head for each. It is trained on both tasks together and produces both outputs for a post while reading it only once.

**Multi-task optimizer.** A training method that controls how the tasks influence the model during training. Equal weighting and tuned static weighting keep the task weights fixed, and the other 11 optimizers adjust the task weights, the task gradients, or both during training. The study compares 13 multi-task optimizers, which Chapter 2 describes.

**Named entity recognition (NER).** The task that finds words or phrases in a post that name specific details, such as places, and assigns each an entity type. It works on parts of a post rather than the whole post.

**Negative transfer.** A drop in predictive performance on a task when a model is trained on both tasks together, compared with the single-task model for that task. It is measured as the change in F1-score, which is the score of the multi-task model minus the score of the single-task model. A negative change shows negative transfer, and a positive change shows positive transfer.

**Peak memory.** The largest amount of GPU memory, the memory of the laptop's graphics processor, that training uses at any one time. Chapter 3 describes how it is measured.

**Post.** A message that a person publishes on social media. The dataset of this study mainly consists of posts on X, formerly Twitter, which were earlier called tweets.

**Predictive performance.** The degree to which a model performs a task correctly on the validation or test posts, measured with F1-scores.

**Pretrained encoder.** The language model, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, that was trained on large amounts of text before this study. It reads every post and converts the text into numbers that the task heads can use, and all models use the same encoder. In the multi-task model, both tasks share it.

**Processing time.** The time that a trained model takes to produce its outputs for the test posts, reported as the mean time per post. For the single-task models, the times of the two models are added. Chapter 3 describes how it is measured.

**Random seed.** A number that fixes the random choices made during training, such as the starting values of the task heads and the order of the training posts. Training with different seeds shows how much the results vary by chance.

**Single-task model.** A model trained on one task only, using the same pretrained encoder as the multi-task model. Its predictive performance serves as the baseline for measuring negative and positive transfer on that task.

**Specialized optimizer.** Any of the 11 multi-task optimizers other than equal weighting and tuned static weighting. These optimizers adjust the task weights, change the task gradients, or do both during training.

**Storage.** The disk space that the files of a trained model take up. For the single-task models, the files of the two models are counted together.

**Taglish.** The mix of Tagalog and English that many Filipinos use in everyday writing, and the language of the posts in the dataset.

**Task gradient.** The signal that one task sends the model during training to indicate how the model should change to reduce its error on that task.

**Task head.** The component of a model that makes the predictions for one task, using the output of the pretrained encoder.

**Task weight.** A number that sets how much one task influences training. During training, the error of the model on each task is multiplied by the task weight of that task before the two are added together.

**Test posts.** Labeled posts that are kept out of training and selection and used only once, to compare the final model with the single-task models.

**Token.** A word or part of a word that the model reads as one unit.

**Training cost.** The training time and peak memory needed to train one model. Since the 13 candidate models share the same pretrained encoder, dataset, and laptop, differences in training cost between them come from their optimizers, as implemented in LibMTL or, for two of them, in the code of this study. It does not include the tuning runs that choose the learning rate and the task weights of tuned static weighting.

**Training settings.** The values that control how a model is trained, such as how many times it goes through the training posts and how much it changes at each step, called the learning rate. All models in this study use the same values, except the learning rate, which is tuned for each model.

**Tuned static weighting.** The multi-task optimizer that keeps the task weights fixed throughout training at values chosen together with the learning rate by testing several options on the validation posts before training, which requires training the model several times.

**Validation posts.** Labeled posts that are kept out of training and used to choose the learning rate of each model, the task weights of tuned static weighting, and the point in each run at which the model is saved, and to select the multi-task optimizer for the final model.
